questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: The acquired forms account for what share of primary hyperaldosteronism (PHA)?
questions.exp: PHA is 90% acquired and 10% familial. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: Match the acquired PHA cause to its frequency — 1) B/L adrenal micronodular hyperplasia  2) U/L adrenal adenoma … A) 30%  B) 60%
questions.exp: Bilateral micronodular hyperplasia is 60%; unilateral adrenal adenoma (Conn's syndrome) is 30%. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: ‘Conn's syndrome’ is the eponym for:
questions.exp: U/L adrenal adenoma (30%) is a.k.a. Conn's syndrome. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: Match familial PHA — 1) Type I  2) Type II … A) ClCN2 mutation  B) Glucocorticoid remediable aldosteronism (GRA), autosomal dominant
questions.exp: Familial (10%): Type I = GRA (AD); Type II = ClCN2 mutation. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: In the cortical collecting duct P-cell, aldosterone acts via MR to induce AIP, which then activates:
questions.exp: MR–Aldo (+) induces AIP (aldosterone-induced protein) which (+) activates ENaC, retaining Na+ and losing K+/H+. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: AIP in the P-cell diagram stands for ___.
questions.exp: AIP = aldosterone-induced protein. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: Despite salt and water retention, PHA causes no edema because:
opts: The retained volume stimulates ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide)
The kidney escapes via pressure natriuresis of the proximal tubule only
questions.exp: Salt & water retention stimulates ANP, so there is no edema. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: The classic triad of PHA is hypertension with:
questions.exp: Triad: HTN, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: In PHA-associated hypertension, the book notes:
questions.exp: The hypertension shows diastolic > systolic. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: Match AME vs GRA — 1) AME inheritance  2) GRA inheritance  3) AME cause  4) GRA cause … A) Autosomal dominant  B) Autosomal recessive  C) 11β-HSD2 defect  D) Chimeric ACTH-driven aldosterone secretion
questions.exp: AME is AR with 11β-HSD2 defect; GRA is AD with a chimeric effect where ACTH drives aldosterone. Both give HTN + mA + hypokalaemia. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Conn's syndrome: classification and pathophysiology · p841
questions.q: ‘GRA is treated with steroids, which suppress the ACTH driving the aldosterone.’
questions.exp: Rx steroids (−) suppress ACTH and hence the chimeric aldosterone secretion in GRA. (Book p841)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: The typical presentation of PHA pairs hypertension with:
opts: Proximal/distal severe muscle weakness and loss of power (fatigue)
questions.exp: HTN with proximal/distal severe muscle weakness + loss of power (fatigue) from hypokalaemia. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Renal potassium loss is confirmed by:
opts: Urine K+/creatinine and a raised urine spot K+
questions.exp: Confirmed by 1. urine K+/creatinine and 2. urine spot K+ ↑. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Match the ABG branch in a hypokalaemic patient — 1) Metabolic acidosis  2) Metabolic alkalosis … A) Leads to the PHA/AME/GRA/Liddle/Cushing work-up  B) Renal tubular acidosis (RTA)
questions.exp: Hypokalaemia with metabolic acidosis → RTA; with metabolic alkalosis → the hyperaldosterone spectrum. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis with NORMAL blood pressure points to:
questions.exp: Note: hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis + normal BP = Gitelman/Bartter syndromes. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Match cause of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with HTN — 1) Acquired  2) Inherited … A) AME (AR), GRA (AD), Liddle (AD)  B) Cushing syndrome and PHA
questions.exp: Acquired: Cushing syndrome, PHA; inherited: AME (AR), GRA (AD), Liddle syndrome (AD). (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Liddle syndrome is caused by:
opts: A gain-of-function mutation of the ENaC channel
questions.exp: Liddle syndrome (AD) = gain-of-function mutation of the ENaC channel. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: ‘The Endocrine Society recommends screening every newly diagnosed hypertensive for PHA, irrespective of age.’
opts: True, but only with a family history
questions.exp: Every newly diagnosed HTN irrespective of age is screened for PHA. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: HTN plus target-organ damage at diagnosis or disproportionate should prompt:
opts: A secondary hypertension work-up unless proven otherwise
questions.exp: HTN + TOD should be considered secondary HTN unless proven otherwise (renal or endocrine cause, incl. PHA). (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Which is NOT listed among the target-organ-damage markers?
questions.exp: TOD = LVH, fundus changes, microalbuminuria, increased central SYSTOLIC BP. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: The old screening method, now obsolete because drugs interfere, was:
questions.exp: ARR is obsolete as drugs interfere with the result. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: Match ARR interference — 1) False positive  2) False negative … A) ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, dihydropyridine CCB  B) β-blocker, NSAIDs, clonidine
questions.exp: False positives: β-blocker, NSAIDs, clonidine; false negatives: ACEi, ARB, spironolactone, dihydropyridine (CCB). (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: While being screened, the patient should be shifted to:
questions.exp: Shift to α-blocker, hydralazine, non-dihydropyridine to avoid interference. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Presentation, screening recommendations and first-line tests · p842
questions.q: The newer screening test on an early-morning sample is positive when PAC and PRA are respectively:
questions.exp: Early morning sample: PAC ≥10 ng/dl and PRA ≤1 ng/ml/hr → proceed to confirmatory test. (Book p842)

questions.sec: Confirmatory testing and lateralisation · p843
questions.q: The confirmatory test for PHA is the saline infusion test, performed as:
opts: Give oral salt load for 3 days
Infuse 2 litres of normal saline over 4 hours
questions.exp: Saline infusion test: infuse 2 litres NS over 4 hr to expand intravascular volume. (Book p843)

questions.sec: Confirmatory testing and lateralisation · p843
questions.q: ‘In PHA the post-saline aldosterone remains unsuppressed (>10 ng/dL); a normal response is a fall in aldosterone.’
questions.exp: Volume expansion suppresses aldosterone normally (−); in PHA it stays >10 ng/dL (+). (Book p843)

questions.sec: Confirmatory testing and lateralisation · p843
questions.q: After a positive screen, 2 L saline is infused over 4 h and the repeat PAC is 14 ng/dL. The next best step is:
opts: Adrenal vein sampling before any imaging
CT abdomen (IOC) to look for B/L hyperplasia vs U/L adenoma
questions.exp: Repeat PAC ≥10 ng/dl confirms PHA; CT abdomen (IOC) then distinguishes B/L hyperplasia from U/L adenoma in the adrenal gland. (Book p843)

questions.sec: Confirmatory testing and lateralisation · p843
questions.q: The imaging of choice to localise the adrenal lesion in confirmed PHA is:
questions.exp: CT abdomen is the IOC, showing either B/L hyperplasia or U/L adenoma. (Book p843)

questions.sec: Confirmatory testing and lateralisation · p843
questions.q: On the confirmatory saline test, a post-infusion PAC above what value supports PHA?
questions.exp: Aldosterone >10 ng/dL after saline (unsuppressed) is positive for PHA. (Book p843)

units.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism: causes and the P-cell mechanism
units.guide: PHA = 90% acquired (B/L micronodular hyperplasia 60%; U/L adenoma 30% = Conn's) + 10% familial (Type I GRA, AD; Type II ClCN2). Aldosterone→MR→AIP (aldosterone-induced protein)→ENaC in P-cells: Na+ in, K+/H+ out; ANP activation explains no edema. Triad HTN (diastolic > systolic) + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. AME (AR, 11β-HSD2 defect) vs GRA (AD, chimeric ACTH-driven aldosterone; Rx steroids).

units.title: Presentation, who to screen and the drug-aware work-up
units.guide: HTN + proximal/distal weakness; confirm renal K+ loss (urine K+/creatinine, spot K+ ↑). ABG: acidosis → RTA; alkalosis → acquired (Cushing, PHA) vs inherited (AME AR, GRA AD, Liddle AD = ENaC gain-of-function). Normal BP + hypokalaemic alkalosis = Gitelman/Bartter. Screen every new HTN; HTN + TOD (LVH, fundus, microalbuminuria, ↑ central systolic BP) → secondary work-up. ARR obsolete; false + β-blocker/NSAIDs/clonidine, false − ACEi/ARB/spironolactone/dihydropyridine; bridge with α-blocker, hydralazine, non-DHP. Screen: PAC ≥10 ng/dl + PRA ≤1 ng/ml/hr.

units.title: Saline infusion confirmation and CT lateralisation
units.guide: Saline infusion test: 2 L NS over 4 h; normal suppression vs PHA unsuppressed (>10 ng/dL). Repeat PAC ≥10 ng/dl → CT abdomen (IOC) → B/L hyperplasia vs U/L adenoma.
